options.text: Check your own side of the process, such as how much notice your orders gave and how often quantities changed after ordering
options.rationale: Short notice and late changes to orders are common causes of late delivery. If the cause is on the buyer's side, no amount of pressure on the supplier will fix it.

options.text: Apply the late-delivery charge from the next delivery, to give the supplier a clear financial reason to improve its performance
options.rationale: The candidate reaches for the contractual lever before knowing the cause. If your own ordering is part of the problem, the charge punishes the wrong party and damages the relationship needed to fix it.

options.text: Add five days of buffer to each future delivery date in the schedule, so that a late delivery no longer delays a changeover
options.rationale: The candidate absorbs the problem instead of removing it. Buffers cost schedule and stock on every delivery and leave the cause of lateness exactly where it was.

options.text: Start qualifying a second film supplier, so that future orders can be moved if the current supplier's performance does not improve
options.rationale: Qualifying a new food-contact packaging supplier is slow and expensive. The candidate commits to it before finding out whether the problem lies with the supplier at all.

questions.explanation: When a supplier's performance is poor across a run of deliveries, improvement starts with a joint look at the data, including the buyer's own part in it, since late orders and changed quantities are frequent causes of late delivery. Penalties, buffers and second sources each have a place, but chosen before the cause is known they either punish the wrong party or hide a problem that could have been removed.
questions.mindset: Find out why a partner is failing, including what you are doing to cause it, before deciding what to do about it.

questions.stem: On a smart-meter programme, three software squads hold fortnightly retrospectives, while the hardware workstream records lessons at its quarterly stage gates. Most of the programme's serious problems in the past six months arose where firmware releases met hardware test schedules, yet these issues rarely appear in either set of records. Each side assumes the other is dealing with them. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Ask the hardware workstream to adopt fortnightly retrospectives, so that its improvement cycle matches the cadence of the software squads
options.rationale: The candidate aligns the cadences but leaves each side reviewing only its own work. Interface problems would still fall between two sets of retrospectives, just more frequent ones.

options.text: Hold a regular cross-workstream retrospective with members of the squads and the hardware team, focused on the interface between them
options.rationale: Problems that arise between teams need a forum where both sides are present. Focusing it on the interface brings the issues each side has assumed the other owns into one discussion.

options.text: Collect the squads' retrospective outputs at each stage gate, and add any interface items to the hardware lessons register for review
options.rationale: The candidate routes interface issues through one side's quarterly process. It is too slow for fortnightly releases and still leaves the software squads out of the review of their own interface problems.

options.text: Keep a shared log of interface issues and improvement actions that both sides can see, with each action assigned to a named owner
options.rationale: The issues go unrecorded because each side assumes the other has them. A shared, visible log with owners removes that assumption and makes interface problems trackable.

options.text: Raise the interface problems with the programme sponsor at the next steering meeting, and ask for a decision on which side should own them
options.rationale: The candidate escalates something within the programme manager's own authority to organise. Interface problems are shared by nature, so assigning them wholesale to one side misreads the cause.

questions.explanation: Improvement routines tend to follow team boundaries, so problems that arise between teams fall outside every team's retrospective and lessons register. In a hybrid environment the seams between delivery methods need their own improvement forum and a shared, visible record, so that issues nobody owns by default are given an owner and acted on.
questions.mindset: Look for improvement where teams meet, because that is where nobody is looking.

questions.stem: Your team on a charity's donations platform wants to reduce cycle time, which averages nine days per story, and proposes splitting stories smaller. On the cycle-time scatterplot for the last three months, you see that most stories finished in four to seven days, but eight stories took between 25 and 40 days, pulling the average up. What should you do first?

options.text: Support the team's proposal to split stories smaller, since smaller stories tend to reduce cycle time and the team is motivated to try it.
options.rationale: The candidate backs a general remedy that targets typical stories, which already finish in under a week. If the eight long stories were held up by something other than size, splitting changes little.

options.text: Look at the eight long-running stories with the team to find out what they had in common, before agreeing on a change to make.
options.rationale: The high average is driven by a few outliers, and outliers usually share a specific cause such as an external dependency or a blocked environment. Finding it points the improvement at what is really pushing cycle time up.

options.text: Report the median cycle time instead of the average, so that the measure reflects typical stories and is not distorted by a few exceptions.
options.rationale: The candidate changes the measure rather than the process. The median would look better immediately while the stories taking five weeks carry on exactly as before.

options.text: Set a work-in-progress limit on the team's board, because cycle time across the board falls when fewer stories are started at the same time.
options.rationale: The candidate applies a sound flow practice without checking it fits the problem. A WIP limit helps when queues are the cause, which nothing yet shows about the eight outliers.

questions.explanation: When a few items take far longer than the rest, they are usually held up by something specific, such as an external dependency, an unclear requirement or a blocked environment, rather than by the way typical work flows. Examine the outliers before choosing a general remedy, because a change aimed at the typical item can leave the real cause of a high average untouched.
questions.mindset: Study the exceptions before changing the rule.
